Mahavira. Meaning great hero, he was the twenty-fourth and final Tirthankara, or ford-maker, of Jainism, who revitalized and systematized the ancient Jain tradition in sixth century BCE India. His ascetic teachings and emphasis on absolute non-violence and truth established Jainism as a major philosophical and religious force in India and beyond. Mahavira was born as Vardhamana, a prince in what is now Bihar, India, around five hundred ninety-nine BCE and renounced his princely life at age thirty to pursue spiritual asceticism. He spent twelve years in extreme self-denial and meditation, eventually achieving kevala jnana, the perfect knowledge that defines a Tirthankara. His teachings emphasize Mahatma, the great soul, through the practice of the Mahavratas, five great vows: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, chastity, and detachment. Ahimsa, non-violence toward all living beings, is the cornerstone of Jain ethics and distinguishes Jainism from other Indian religious traditions. Mahavira taught that every soul is eternal and capable of achieving liberation through rigorous asceticism and moral discipline, regardless of caste or birth. He established the Jain monastic community, the Sangha, with strict codes of conduct that remain influential in Jain practice today. The Jina, or conqueror, title applied to him reflects his spiritual victory over worldly attachments and ignorance, and his life and teachings are celebrated annually on Mahavira Jayanti.
